sections.html: Xenopus tropicalis (often called Silurana tropicalis) is clearly different from Xenopus laevis. It grows only about 4 cm (X. laevis up to 15 cm), has smaller eyes and is a tropical species that could never survive a European winter. Care is simple.

The trade of clawed frogs of the species Xenopus laevis will most likely soon be banned because a reproducing population has been discovered in France. Due to climate change, it is feared that this species could become invasive in Europe. To prevent this, the trade with this species should be prohibited.

Some strains of Xenopus laevis come from South Africa and can even survive sub-zero temperatures for short periods. X. tropicalis is obtained both as wild catch from Nigeria and as EU offspring or from Southeast Asia. Because of the good suitability of this small species for community aquariums with fish, it has largely replaced its larger cousin in breeding for aquarium purposes. X. laevis is mainly bred as a laboratory animal for medical research, and animals from these breedings have sometimes entered the pet trade.

Occasionally the small (around 6 cm) Xenopus muelleri is also available as offspring. This tropical species remains allowed.

It is very important to cover the aquarium completely. In case of air pressure fluctuations, the animals are overcome by a great wandering instinct and become perfect escape artists. Unfortunately, such excursions in living rooms usually end fatally.
It eats and tolerates any ornamental fish food, whether dry, frozen or live.
It is peaceful, but will try to eat anything that fits in its mouth. Therefore fish kept together with X. tropicalis should not be smaller than 3 cm.
